p01.why: The using declaration brings in both overloads declared before it, so f(1) gives 1 and f(1.5) gives 2.

p02.why: The out-of-namespace definition of N::f is in M, which does not enclose N.

p03.why: A using declaration must not name a namespace.

p04.why: The first name in a nested namespace path must not be inline.

p05.why: N::x is defined outside N without a declaration in N first.

p06.why: L is a second name for the nested namespace, so L::x is 6.

p07.why: A namespace definition must be at namespace scope, not in a function body.

p08.why: A repeated using declaration in a block: Clang 22, Clang 18 and GCC 16 accept, GCC 14 and EDG 7.0 reject (Q-0019); the provisional answer is that it compiles.

p09.why: The global int x conflicts with the using declaration of x in the same scope.

p10.why: The using declaration carries only f(int), declared before it, so f(1.5) converts to int and returns 1.

p11.why: A using declaration can list several names; x + y is 3.

p12.why: A namespace definition must not use an alias to reopen the namespace.

p13.why: The nested path defines A, B and C in order, and the assertion holds.

p14.why: The namespace N has the name of a variable in the same scope.

p15.why: x is a member of N and is named without one of the allowed forms.

p16.why: The alias L is made to name a different namespace in the same scope.

p17.why: The directive ends with the function body, so x at global scope is not visible.

p18.why: count was first declared with external linkage, so a later static definition is not valid.

p19.why: The directive makes N::x visible to unqualified lookup.

p20.why: Members of namespaces named by directives inside B become visible too, so x finds A::x.

p21.why: The second definition of N adds y, and x is visible inside N.

p22.why: V was first defined without inline and must not later be defined with inline.

p23.why: Both members are declared in N first and defined outside with qualified names; there is no main.

p24.why: Lib::version finds the inline V2 member, and V1 is reached only by its own name.

p25.why: Members of an unnamed namespace are usable without qualification.

p26.why: The using declaration of x conflicts with the global x declared before it.

p27.why: Inside N the name v finds N::v, and ::v names the global one.

p28.why: A using declaration at namespace scope must not name a class member.

p29.why: Members declared after the directive are visible too; 1 + 4 is 5.

p30.why: x is declared in the inline namespace and in A, so A::x is ambiguous.

p31.why: A later definition of the inline namespace can omit inline, and its members are still members of A.

p32.why: Two directives make x ambiguous, and x is used.

p33.why: inline is allowed after the first name in the path, so x is a member of A and of A::V1.

p34.why: A using directive must not occur in a class.

p35.why: z is in the unnamed namespace and in the global namespace, so the unqualified use is ambiguous.

p36.why: A using declaration must have a qualified name.

p37.why: extern and static on the qualified definitions match the first declarations, so both checks pass and main returns 0.

p38.why: A using directive must name a namespace, and S is a class.

p39.why: The same using declaration can occur again in the same scope; at namespace scope the Evidence records no divergence.

p40.why: The directive puts N::v at global level for lookup, beside the global v, so v is ambiguous.

p41.why: A::x is qualified, so the ambiguity from the two directives does not arise.

p42.why: The using declaration makes x name N::x.

p43.why: The local x declared in the function hides N::x, so f() returns 2.
